pos: n. (in the Authorized Version rendering chiefly Hebrew 'ēth and mō'ēd, and Greek chronos (duration) and kairos (the appointed season))
etymology: From Old English tīma, a limited space of duration, cognate with Old Norse tīmi and ultimately with tide — that which is measured out, portioned, allotted. The root sense is not bare succession but allotment: a stretch of duration cut off and given. That is precisely the biblical sense. Scripture has no word for abstract empty time flowing on of itself; it speaks of times that are given, appointed, fulfilled, and ended. The Greek makes the distinction the English blurs: chronos is duration measured, kairos is the fit and appointed moment, and the Authorized Version renders both by this one word.
biblical_def: Time is the creature's measure, made by God when He made the world, and wholly under His government. It is not a vessel God inhabits but a thing He ordained: the lights were set in the firmament “for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years,” and duration itself began when the heaven and the earth began. God Himself is eternal, without succession, inhabiting eternity; He does not wait, and nothing overtakes Him. But everything He has made lives under measure, and that measure is His. The Preacher lays down the rule — “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1) — and the appointed purpose is God's, not the creature's. David draws the pastoral comfort out of it in four words: “My times are in thy hand” (Psa 31:15). Not his time, but his times — the plural of every allotted season of a life, each one held. The redemptive centre of the doctrine is Gal 4:4: the Son was sent not early and not late but when the fulness of the time was come, which means the whole calendar of empires, exiles, and generations was a clock running to one hour. And because the days are evil, the believer is commanded to buy up the time (Eph 5:16) — to treat it as a purchased commodity, spent on account before God.
webster_summary: A limited portion of duration, measured out and allotted by the Creator; in Scripture never bare succession but a season given, appointed, filled, and ended by God, in whose hand every creature's times are held.
webster_full: TIME, n. 1. A particular portion or part of duration, whether past, present or future. The time was; the time has been; the time is; the time will be. Lo, the time is at hand.

2. A proper time; a season. There is a time to every purpose under heaven. Ecclesiastes 3. Webster's second sense is the biblical one: not duration in the abstract, but the fit and appointed occasion.
3. Duration. God, whose eternal duration is not to be measured, is said to inhabit eternity; time is the measure of things that begin and end, and therefore of the creature only.

4. A season; the state of things at a particular period. The times are evil. Hence the apostolic charge to redeem the time, that is, to buy it up as a merchant buys goods at market, because the season of opportunity is short.

5. Repetition of anything, or mention with reference to repetition. Four times; ten times. From this comes the common reckoning of times and half a time in the prophets, where a set and bounded period is intended.
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
Psalm 31:15
My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.
Ephesians 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Galatians 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
corruption_summary: Modern thought empties time of appointment and leaves only succession — a blind river carrying men nowhere — and then, having removed the Appointer, tells the creature that the moment belongs to him and must be seized before it is gone.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing modern assumption is that time is autonomous: an empty container running on by itself, indifferent to purpose, in which things merely happen. Strip the doctrine of providence out of duration and two errors follow at once. The first is fatalism — if the river carries everything and no one steers it, then nothing that happens means anything, which is the settled despair beneath a great deal of contemporary art and manner. The second is its mirror, the frantic self-assertion of carpe diem: if no one has appointed my season, I must seize it myself, and every hour not spent on my own advancement is an hour lost. Scripture cuts under both. The times are appointed, and they are appointed by a Person, and that Person is a Father to His people.

There is a second and subtler corruption inside the church — the treatment of one's own remaining time as an assumed possession. The rich fool did not deny God; he simply spoke of many years he had not been given (Luk 12:20), and that presumption was reckoned folly on the night it was answered. James names the same sin in ordinary speech: to say we will go into such a city and continue there a year, when we know not what shall be on the morrow, is to boast. The remedy is not anxiety but reckoning — asking God to teach us to number our days, so that the hours are spent as what they are, borrowed and accountable.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ēth is the general word for a season or occasion; mō'ēd is the set time, the appointed meeting, from which the feasts take their name. Greek divides duration (chronos) from the fit moment (kairos), and the New Testament's decisive statements about redemption use the second.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ēth (H6256) — time, season, occasion; the ordinary word, used of the time of harvest, the time of rain, the time of the singing of birds. Some 296 occurrences.
Hebrew mō'ēd (H4150) — an appointed time, a set feast, a place or time of meeting; the root of the tabernacle's name, the tent of meeting. Time as summons rather than as duration.
Hebrew yōm (H3117) — day; frequently rendered time where a period rather than a solar day is meant, as in “in the days of Noah.”
Greek chronos (G5550) — duration, extent of time, the quantity that clocks measure; the source of English chronology. Used of the times and seasons the Father has put in His own power (Act 1:7).

Greek kairos (G2540) — the fit, decisive, opportune moment; the season ripe for action. This is the word behind the command to redeem the time, and behind the Lord's statement that His time was not yet come.
usage: Of the appointed hour of redemption: the fulness of the time (Gal 4:4), the due time (Rom 5:6), the accepted time (2Co 6:2) — all of one determinate, sovereign appointment.
Of a bounded prophetic period: a time, times, and the dividing of time (Dan 7:25; Rev 12:14), where the word denotes a set and limited term, not an indefinite stretch.
Of the creature's allotment under providence: “My times are in thy hand” (Psa 31:15); “his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee” (Job 14:5).

etymology: From Old English gēar, common Germanic, cognate with Greek hōra (season, hour) — the root idea being the completed circuit of the seasons and the return of the sun to its place. The Hebrew shānâh comes from a root meaning to repeat or do again, and so names the year by its most obvious property: it comes round. Scripture's year is agricultural and covenantal before it is astronomical — reckoned by seedtime and harvest, and marked out by feasts that God Himself appointed.
biblical_def: The year is the great revolving measure of the creature's life, ordained at creation when God set lights in the firmament for signs and for seasons. In Israel the year was not a neutral calendar but a catechism. God reset its beginning at the Exodus — “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exo 12:2) — so that the nation's reckoning of time itself began at redemption; every subsequent year was counted from the night the blood was on the door. Within the year stood the appointed feasts, and over the years stood the sabbath year, when the land itself rested, and the fiftieth or jubile year, when liberty was proclaimed throughout the land and every man returned unto his possession (Lev 25:10). The year was thus a standing sermon on grace: debts cancelled, inheritances restored, bondage ended, not because the debtor had earned it but because the LORD had appointed a year of release. Isaiah gathers all of it into a Messianic title, “the acceptable year of the LORD” (Isa 61:2), which the Lord Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied to Himself. Set against this is the brevity of the creature's own tale of years — threescore years and ten, and if by strength fourscore, yet their strength is labour and sorrow (Psa 90:10). The year both measures our life and outlasts it.
webster_summary: The period of the earth's revolution, reckoned in Scripture by seedtime and harvest and by the feasts God appointed; the covenantal measure of Israel's life, containing the sabbath year and the jubile, and the standing measure of the brevity of man.
webster_full: YEAR, n. 1. The period of time in which the sun returns to the same point in the ecliptic, or the period in which the earth completes its revolution about the sun.

2. In Scripture, the year is reckoned from the month Abib or Nisan, which God appointed to be the beginning of months at the departure from Egypt. The civil year began in Tisri, the seventh month; the sacred year at the Passover.
3. Years, in the plural, denotes age, or old age. He is a man in years. The days of the years of my pilgrimage. Genesis 47.

4. Sabbatical year; the seventh year, in which the Israelites were commanded to let the land rest, neither sowing the field nor pruning the vineyard, the LORD undertaking to command his blessing on the sixth.
5. Year of jubile; the fiftieth year, in which liberty was proclaimed to all the inhabitants of the land, servants released, and possessions reverting to their ancient owners. Levit. 25.
scriptures: Leviticus 25:10

And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
Isaiah 61:2
To proclaim the acceptable year of the LORD, and the day of vengeance of our God; to comfort all that mourn;
Psalm 90:10
The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
Deuteronomy 11:12
A land which the LORD thy God careth for: the eyes of the LORD thy God are always upon it, from the beginning of the year even unto the end of the year.
corruption_summary: The modern year is a unit of production and self-improvement, measured by what a man got done in it; the biblical year is a unit of accountability and release, measured by what God appointed in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The calendar is never doctrinally neutral, and the reordering of the year is one of the quietest ways a people is discipled. Israel's year began at redemption and was punctuated by feasts commemorating God's acts; the commercial year now begins at a fiscal quarter and is punctuated by seasons of purchase. What is lost is not sentiment but instruction. A year framed by Passover and atonement teaches a nation that it exists by deliverance and needs a covering for sin; a year framed by resolutions in January teaches that a man is his own project and the deficiency is one of discipline. The remedy is not a scheme of new holy days — the regulative principle governs the church's worship, and the Lord's Day is the weekly appointment God has actually given — but a household reckoning of the year under providence rather than under productivity.

The jubile is the point at which the modern instinct most plainly fails. Lev 25 makes release a matter of divine appointment rather than of the creditor's generosity or the debtor's merit: at the sound of the trumpet the land returned, because the land was the LORD's and the men were His servants, not their own. That is a picture of the gospel, and it cannot be reduced to a programme of economic policy without losing precisely what it teaches. The acceptable year of the LORD which Christ proclaimed is not an improved arrangement of debts; it is the liberty of captives whose ransom another has paid in full.
roots_summary: Hebrew shānâh names the year from a root meaning to repeat — the returning circuit. Greek etos is the ordinary year of reckoning; eniautos tends toward the year as a completed cycle, and is the word used of the acceptable year and of the high priest's yearly entrance.
roots_lines: Hebrew shānâh (H8141) — year; from shānâh (H8138), to repeat or do again, naming the year by its recurrence. Some 875 occurrences.
Hebrew yōbēl (H3104) — jubile; properly the blast of a ram's horn, and so the year announced by that blast, the fiftieth.
Hebrew shēmīttâh — the release of the seventh year (Deu 15:1), from a root meaning to let drop or let fall; the debt is not collected but let go.
Greek etos (G2094) — year, the plain unit of reckoning; used of the woman with an issue of blood twelve years, and of the thousand years of Rev 20.
Greek eniautos (G1763) — a year viewed as a completed cycle; used in Luk 4:19 of the acceptable year of the Lord and in Heb 9:7 of the yearly Day of Atonement.
usage: Of the covenantal calendar: the beginning of months at the Exodus (Exo 12:2), the three yearly feasts (Exo 23:14), the sabbath year and the jubile (Lev 25).
Of age and the span of life: the days of the years of a pilgrimage (Gen 47:9); threescore years and ten (Psa 90:10); Methuselah's nine hundred sixty and nine years (Gen 5:27).
Of the Messianic proclamation: the acceptable year of the LORD (Isa 61:2), read by Christ at Nazareth and declared fulfilled in the hearing of the synagogue.

etymology: From Old English mōnaþ, directly from mōna, the moon — the month is the moon's period, and the two words are one word in nearly every language that has them. The Hebrew keeps the same tie twice over: yerach is a month and yārēach is the moon, while the commoner chōdesh comes from a root meaning new and names the month by its first sight of the new crescent. Israel's month therefore began with an observation and a trumpet, not with a printed page.
biblical_def: The month is the lunar measure God appointed within the year, and in Israel it was the hinge on which the whole calendar of worship turned. Because chōdesh means the new, the month opened at the new moon, and the beginnings of months were themselves marked with the blowing of trumpets over the burnt offerings and peace offerings, “that they may be to you for a memorial before your God” (Num 10:10). The reckoning of months was reset at the redemption from Egypt: “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you” (Exo 12:2). Abib, the month of green ears, became the first, and Passover fell within it, so that the nation could not name a month without counting from deliverance. The months carried the feasts — unleavened bread in the first, weeks in the third, trumpets and atonement and tabernacles in the seventh — and thus the year taught doctrine in order. Scripture also uses the month as the plain measure of a determined life: “the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass” (Job 14:5). At the last, in the city where there is no need of the sun, the tree of life yields her fruit every month (Rev 22:2) — the measure remains, but it now measures unfailing supply rather than decay.
webster_summary: The period of the moon's revolution, and in Israel the unit that began at the new moon with trumpets; the ordering measure of the appointed feasts, reset to begin at the Exodus, and a common Scripture measure of an appointed span of life.
webster_full: MONTH, n. A space or period of time constituting a division of the year. The month is lunar or solar. The lunar month is the time in which the moon passes from one conjunction with the sun to another.
2. The Jews reckoned by lunar months, beginning at the appearance of the new moon, which was announced by the sound of trumpets and marked by appointed sacrifices. Numbers 10.
3. The sacred year of the Hebrews began with Abib or Nisan, in which the passover was kept; this order was appointed at the deliverance from Egypt. Exodus 12.
4. Months, in the plural, is used for an appointed or measured term of life or of affliction. The number of his months are with thee. Job 14.
5. The word is derived immediately from moon, the two being one in origin; and so in the Hebrew, where yerach is a month and yareach the moon.
scriptures: Exodus 12:2
This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you.
Numbers 10:10

Also in the day of your gladness, and in your solemn days, and in the beginnings of your months, ye shall blow with the trumpets over your burnt offerings, and over the sacrifices of your peace offerings; that they may be to you for a memorial before your God: I am the LORD your God.
Job 14:5
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
Revelation 22:2

In the midst of the street of it, and on either side of the river, was there the tree of life, which bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month: and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.
corruption_summary: The month has been flattened from an appointed marker of worship into an administrative square on a grid, and where it is invested with meaning again the meaning is astrological rather than covenantal.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors attend the month. The first is emptying: the month becomes a billing period and nothing more, a unit of rent and payroll with no memorial in it. Israel could not begin a month without trumpets and a burnt offering, which meant the passage of time itself was referred to God and covered by sacrifice; the modern month refers to nothing and is covered by nothing. The second error is refilling the emptied month with the wrong content. Where men will not have the appointed feasts they take up the zodiac, and the naming of months and the reading of birth-months for character and destiny is the old Chaldean art in a magazine column. Scripture forbids it plainly — Israel was warned against those that are astrologers and monthly prognosticators (Isa 47:13), and the warning has not lapsed.

There is also a churchly error worth naming: the assumption that because the Old Testament calendar was appointed by God, the church is bound to reproduce a monthly cycle of holy days. Colossians answers it directly — let no man judge you in respect of the new moon or of the sabbath days, which are a shadow of things to come, the body being Christ's. The shadow has met its substance. Under the regulative principle the church keeps the day the Lord has given, the first day of the week, and does not multiply appointed seasons of its own devising.
roots_summary: The Hebrew names the month twice, once from the moon (yerach) and once from newness (chōdesh, the new moon and so the month it opens). Greek mēn is cognate with the same Indo-European root that gives moon and measure.
roots_lines: Hebrew chōdesh (H2320) — the new moon, and by extension the month it begins; from chādash (H2318), to be new, to renew. Some 276 occurrences.
Hebrew yerach (H3391) — month, the lunar period; directly related to yārēach (H3394), the moon. The older and more poetic of the two words.
Hebrew ābīb (H24) — the month of green ears, the first month of the sacred year, later called Nisan; the name is agricultural, marking barley in the ear.
Greek mēn (G3376) — month; used of Elisabeth's hiding five months and of the forty and two months of Rev 11:2.
Greek neomēnia (G3561) — new moon; the term in Col 2:16 among the shadows fulfilled in Christ.
usage: Of the covenant calendar reset at redemption: the beginning of months (Exo 12:2), from which Passover, unleavened bread, and the whole festal order are counted.
Of the appointed span of a life or an affliction: the number of his months are with thee (Job 14:5); Jephthah's daughter bewailing two months (Jdg 11:38).
Of prophetic periods reckoned in months: forty and two months (Rev 11:2; 13:5), the same determined term expressed elsewhere in days and in times.

pos: n. (rendering Hebrew shābua', a seven, and Greek sabbaton in the idiom “the first day of the week”)
etymology: From Old English wice, common Germanic, with an underlying sense of turning or succession — the round that comes back to its start. The Hebrew is franker: shābua' simply means a seven, from the numeral seven, so that in Hebrew one does not speak of a week but of a sevening. This matters for prophecy, where the seventy weeks of Dan 9 are seventy sevens, and the unit counted may be years rather than days. The Greek of the Gospels uses sabbaton, the sabbath, for the whole period, reckoning the week by the day that closes it.
biblical_def: The week is the one division of time that has no basis in the motions of the heavens. Months follow the moon and years follow the sun, but nothing in the sky marks off seven days; the week rests solely on the creation ordinance, on God's working six days and resting the seventh, and on the fourth commandment which binds the creature to the same rhythm. It is therefore a standing witness against the notion that time is merely astronomical, and a standing testimony to the God who made and hallowed it. Jacob's service for Rachel is measured by it — “Fulfil her week” (Gen 29:27) — and the marriage feast ran seven days. The Pharisee's boast is measured by it: “I fast twice in the week” (Luk 18:12), a piety kept by the calendar and offered to God as a claim. The prophetic sevens of Dan 9:27 set the covenant confirmed and the sacrifice caused to cease within one week, the hinge of the seventy. And in the New Testament the week's weight shifts to its first day: Christ rose on the first day of the week, the disciples came together on it to break bread, and the collection was appointed on it, so that the Lord's Day now stands where the seventh once stood — not the abolition of the ordinance but its resurrection ordering.
webster_summary: The period of seven days, resting on no motion of sun or moon but on the creation ordinance and the fourth commandment; closed in Israel by the sabbath, and opened in the church by the Lord's Day, the first day of the week on which Christ rose.
webster_full: WEEK, n. The space of seven days. The Hebrews reckoned by weeks from the beginning, the seventh day being appointed for rest at the creation and afterward commanded in the law.
2. In Scripture the word answers to the Hebrew shabua, a seven; and in the prophets a week may denote seven years, as in the seventy weeks of Daniel.
3. Feast of weeks; the second of the three great feasts, kept seven weeks after the passover, called also Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day.
4. The first day of the week; the day on which our Lord rose from the dead, and on which the disciples came together to break bread and to lay by them in store. Acts 20; 1 Cor. 16.
5. Unlike the month and the year, the week has no ground in the courses of the heavenly bodies, but stands wholly upon the divine appointment at the creation.
scriptures: Genesis 29:27
Fulfil her week, and we will give thee this also for the service which thou shalt serve with me yet seven other years.
Daniel 9:27

And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate.
Luke 18:12
I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.
Isaiah 66:23
And it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another, shall all flesh come to worship before me, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The week is treated as a human convention that may be redrawn for convenience, and its seventh part — the day of rest and worship — is absorbed into labour and leisure until nothing in the seven is set apart to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the week alone among the divisions of time has no astronomical footing, it is the first thing revolutionary régimes attack. The French republican calendar imposed a ten-day décade and the early Soviet nepreryvka a staggered five-day cycle, in both cases with the express purpose of dissolving the day of worship by making congregations impossible to gather. Both failed and were abandoned, which is itself a testimony. The modern attack is milder and far more effective: the week is left intact on paper while its seventh part is quietly filled with commerce, sport, and overtime, so that the ordinance is kept in name and broken in substance. The creature who will not rest is not free; he has merely changed masters.

A second corruption runs the other way, and the Lord addressed it directly in the parable of the Pharisee: “I fast twice in the week.” A week kept with rigour can become the instrument of self-righteousness, the calendar turned into a ledger of merit presented to God. Both errors miss what the week is for. It was made for man, given as mercy to a creature who must stop, and it points beyond itself to the rest that remains for the people of God, which is entered by faith and not by observance.
roots_summary: Hebrew shābua' is literally a seven, from the numeral, and can denote seven days or seven years according to context. The New Testament idiom for the week is sabbaton, naming the whole from the sabbath, whence “the first day of the week” is literally the first of the sabbaths.
roots_lines: Hebrew shābua' (H7620) — a seven, a period of seven; used of the week of a marriage feast, of the feast of weeks, and of the seventy sevens of Dan 9:24.
Hebrew sheba' (H7651) — seven; the numeral behind the word, itself tied to shāba', to swear, since an oath was sevened or confirmed by seven.
Hebrew shabbāth (H7676) — sabbath, the seventh day of rest; from shābath, to cease, to desist — the day named not for idleness but for ceasing from one's own works.
Greek sabbaton (G4521) — sabbath, and by idiom the week; “the first day of the week” in Mat 28:1 and Act 20:7 is literally the first of the sabbaths.
Greek pentēkostē (G4005) — Pentecost, the fiftieth day; the feast of weeks counted seven sevens from the wave sheaf, the week's rhythm raised to its own square.
usage: Of an ordinary period of seven days: the week of a marriage feast (Gen 29:27); the days of unleavened bread.
Of prophetic sevens of years: the seventy weeks determined upon Daniel's people (Dan 9:24-27), where the unit is plainly not a week of days.
Of the Christian assembly: the first day of the week, on which the disciples came together to break bread (Act 20:7) and were charged to lay by in store (1Co 16:2).

etymology: From Old French houre, from Latin hōra, from Greek hōra — a season, a period, a fit time, and only later a twelfth part of the day. The Greek word never wholly lost the older sense, which is why the New Testament can use it both for a measured sixty minutes and for the appointed moment. Hebrew has no word for hour at all; the Old Testament divides the day by morning, noon, and evening, and by the watches of the night. The term enters Scripture in Daniel, in Aramaic, and becomes common only in the Gospels, where the Roman and Greek reckoning of twelve hours from sunrise was in ordinary use.
biblical_def: The hour is the smallest of the common Scripture measures, and its chief theological weight lies in the second of its two senses. In the plain sense it is the twelfth part of the daylight — “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” — so that the third hour is mid-morning, the sixth noon, and the ninth mid-afternoon, which is why the darkness at the crucifixion from the sixth to the ninth hour covers precisely the brightest part of the day. In the graver sense the hour is the appointed crisis. Throughout John's Gospel the Lord speaks of mine hour: it is not yet come at Cana (Joh 2:4), it is not yet come when they seek to take Him, and then at last it is come, and He says, Father, save me from this hour, but for this cause came I unto this hour. The whole of redemption narrows to a single appointed hour, and He walks toward it deliberately. From this comes the hour's pastoral use as the test of watchfulness: the disciples could not watch with Him one hour (Mat 26:40), and the day and hour of the Lord's return are hidden from men and angels alike (Mat 24:36) precisely so that every hour shall be kept in readiness. To the faithful church at Philadelphia the promise is deliverance out of the hour of temptation (Rev 3:10). The hour is short enough that no man can plead its length, and appointed enough that no man can hasten it.
webster_summary: The twelfth part of the daylight in Scripture reckoning, and by extension the appointed and decisive moment; used of the crisis of Christ's passion, of the hidden day and hour of His coming, and of the brief span in which watchfulness is required.
webster_full: HOUR, n. 1. A space of time equal to one twenty fourth part of the natural day; sixty minutes.

2. In Scripture, the twelfth part of the artificial day, reckoned from sunrise; hence the third hour answers to nine in the morning, the sixth to noon, the ninth to three in the afternoon. Are there not twelve hours in the day? John 11.
3. A particular time; a set or appointed season. Mine hour is not yet come. John 2. In this sense the word denotes not the length of the space but the fitness of the moment.
4. The time of extremity or of death. The hour of temptation; the hour of judgment; the hour is come, glorify thy Son.
5. Hours, in the plural, the stated times of prayer; the third, sixth and ninth hours were so observed by the Jews, and Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour. Acts 10.
scriptures: Matthew 24:36
But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
John 2:4
Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
Matthew 26:40
And he cometh unto the disciples, and findeth them asleep, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour?
Revelation 3:10
Because thou hast kept the word of my patience, I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth.
corruption_summary: The hidden day and hour is the plainest of the Lord's statements and the most persistently ignored, as date-setters keep announcing what the Son says the angels do not know; the opposite error empties the hour of urgency altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 24:36 is unambiguous, and the history of date-setting is a history of men treating it as a puzzle rather than a prohibition. William Miller's 1844, the Watchtower's successive dates, and the periodic paperback calculations of our own time all share one method: a chronological scheme is imposed on apocalyptic numbers, and the plain words are set aside as though they applied only to the era before the scheme was discovered. The damage is not merely the embarrassment of the failed date; it is that the disappointed are taught to despise the doctrine itself. Scripture's reason for hiding the hour is pastoral — watch therefore, for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come — and a known date would destroy the very watchfulness the doctrine exists to produce.

The opposite corruption is quieter and more common in settled churches: the hour that never comes. Where the second coming is treated as a symbol of moral progress or as an indefinite horizon that recedes forever, the summons to watch loses all content, and the parable of the servant who said in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming, is fulfilled without anyone noticing. Both errors can be answered from the same text. The hour is genuinely appointed, genuinely near in the only sense that matters to a mortal creature, and genuinely hidden; and the appointed response is neither calculation nor indifference but readiness.
roots_summary: Greek hōra carries both senses at once — a measured twelfth of the day and the fit or fated moment — and the New Testament exploits both. Hebrew has no equivalent term; the Old Testament divides the day by watches and by the times of the daily sacrifice.
roots_lines: Greek hōra (G5610) — hour, season, the fit moment; some 106 occurrences, from the plain third and sixth hour to the solemn “the hour is come” of Joh 17:1.
Aramaic shā'âh (H8160) — hour, moment; the word in Daniel, as when Nebuchadnezzar's countenance was changed and Daniel was astonied for one hour (Dan 4:19).
Hebrew 'ashmōreth (H821) — a watch of the night; the Old Testament's working division of the dark hours, three in Hebrew reckoning and four in Roman.
Greek phulakē (G5438) — a watch; used in the fourth watch of the night (Mat 14:25), the Roman division the Gospels assume.
Greek stigmē (G4743) — a point, an instant; used only in Luk 4:5, of the moment in which all the kingdoms were shewed — the hour compressed to a point.
usage: Of clock reckoning in the Gospel narratives: the sixth hour at Jacob's well (Joh 4:6); darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour at the crucifixion (Mat 27:45).
Of the appointed crisis of redemption: mine hour is not yet come (Joh 2:4); the hour is come, glorify thy Son (Joh 17:1).
Of eschatological watchfulness: of that day and hour knoweth no man (Mat 24:36); the hour of temptation (Rev 3:10); it is high time to awake out of sleep (Rom 13:11).

pos: n. (the following day; in the Authorized Version chiefly rendering Hebrew mochorāth and Greek aurion)
etymology: From Middle English morwe, from Old English morgen, morning — the same word that gives morning, narrowed to mean the morning next following, and so the next day. The Authorized Version prints it as two words in the idiom to morrow, which is simply on the morrow. The Hebrew mochorāth likewise derives from a root meaning after or behind: the morrow is what comes behind today, and what a man does not yet possess.
biblical_def: The morrow is Scripture's standing name for the future that belongs to God and not to us. Doctrinally it is the point at which the doctrine of providence meets the ordinary conduct of a life, and Scripture presses it from two sides. Against anxiety, the Lord commands, “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself” (Mat 6:34) — not that the believer should be improvident, for the ant provideth her meat in the summer, but that he should not carry tomorrow's burden with today's strength, since grace is issued daily like manna and will not be hoarded. Against presumption, James asks what our life is and answers that it is a vapour, appearing for a little time and vanishing away, so that to speak of tomorrow's business without if the Lord will is not planning but boasting (Jas 4:14). Solomon says the same in a proverb: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). The rich fool is the parable of the sin — he had many goods laid up for many years, and the years were not his to lay up (Luk 12:20). The two commands hold together perfectly. Because the morrow is God's, I need not fear it; and because the morrow is God's, I may not presume upon it.
webster_summary: The next following day; in Scripture the emblem of the future which belongs to God alone, forbidden as an object of anxious care and equally forbidden as a ground of boasting, since no man knows what a day may bring forth.
webster_full: MORROW, n. The day next after the present. To morrow, that is, on the morrow; the following day.
2. In Scripture, the morrow is used for the near and uncertain future. Boast not thyself of to morrow, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. Prov. 27.
3. The word is from the Saxon morgen, morning; the morrow is properly the next morning, and thence the next day. Good morrow, a salutation, is a wish of a good morning.
4. On the morrow; a frequent phrase of narration, marking the next stage of an action. On the morrow, when they were come from Bethany. Mark 11.
5. To take no thought for the morrow is not to forbid forecast and industry, which the Scripture elsewhere commends, but to forbid distrustful and anxious care for what is not yet given.
scriptures: Matthew 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
James 4:14
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
Proverbs 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
Luke 12:20
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
corruption_summary: The command not to take thought for the morrow is read as a licence for improvidence on one side and dismissed as impractical sentiment on the other, while the presumption James actually condemns — planning the future as though it were owned — is celebrated as vision.
corruption_paragraphs: Mat 6:34 suffers two opposite misreadings. Some take it to forbid all forecast, saving, insurance, and provision, which sets the Lord against Solomon, who sends the sluggard to the ant, and against Paul, who says a man that provideth not for his own has denied the faith. The Authorized Version's take no thought meant in 1611 what we should now call be not anxious; the sin forbidden is distrustful care, not prudence. Others, seeing the excess of the first reading, quietly set the verse aside as unworkable in a world of mortgages and pensions. Both miss the promise the command rests on: your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things. Provision is a duty; anxiety is unbelief about a Father who has already undertaken.

The presumption side of the doctrine is scarcely resisted at all, because our age has made it a virtue. To speak confidently of what one will build in five years, without reference to whether one will be alive to build it, is called ambition and taught as a discipline. James calls it rejoicing in one's boastings, and adds that all such rejoicing is evil. The correction he gives is not paralysis but a phrase: if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that. It costs nothing to say and it reorders everything, because it confesses in ordinary speech that the morrow is not a possession but a gift not yet given.
roots_summary: Hebrew mochorāth names the next day from a root meaning after. Greek aurion is the ordinary word for tomorrow, and the New Testament's decisive uses of it are all warnings — against anxiety, against boasting, and against the delay of repentance.
roots_lines: Hebrew māchār (H4279) — to morrow, in time to come; from a root meaning to be after or behind. Used in Exo 8:10, “Be it according to thy word,” where Pharaoh chooses to morrow over today.
Hebrew mochorāth (H4283) — the morrow, the day following; the narrative form, as in the morrow after the passover (Jos 5:11).
Greek aurion (G839) — to morrow, the next day; the word of Mat 6:34 and Jas 4:13, and of the good Samaritan's provision on the morrow (Luk 10:35).
Greek epaurion (G1887) — on the morrow; the narrative connective that carries the Gospel of John through its opening week (Joh 1:29, 35, 43).
Greek atmis (G822) — a vapour, a mist; the figure James sets against the morrow — a life that appeareth for a little time and then vanisheth away.
usage: As plain narrative sequence: on the morrow, when they were come from Bethany (Mar 11:12); the morrow after the passover (Jos 5:11).
As the object of forbidden anxiety: take therefore no thought for the morrow (Mat 6:34), where the Lord grounds the command on the Father's knowledge of our need.
As the object of forbidden presumption: boast not thyself of to morrow (Pro 27:1); ye know not what shall be on the morrow (Jas 4:14); Pharaoh's fatal choice of to morrow for deliverance (Exo 8:10).

etymology: From Old English sunne, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root shared with Latin sōl and Greek hēlios. The Hebrew shemesh is the plain name of the luminary, and it is worth noting what Genesis does not say: in a world where every neighbouring nation named the sun as a god — Shamash in Babylon, Ra in Egypt — Moses declines to name it at all on the fourth day, calling it merely “the greater light to rule the day.” The omission is deliberate polemic. The sun is a lamp, hung by God, and given a job.
biblical_def: The sun is a creature, made on the fourth day, set in the firmament to divide day from night, to rule the day, and to serve for signs and seasons. Scripture's first doctrine of the sun is therefore a demotion: the object the nations worshipped is a servant, and the light it gives was already made on the first day without it. Under this creaturely government it becomes the great figure of God's constancy and impartial common goodness — He “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good” (Mat 5:45), a mercy shed on those who blaspheme Him as freely as on those who bless Him. To Israel the sun is also a figure of God Himself in His giving: “For the LORD God is a sun and shield” (Psa 84:11), light and defence together. The prophetic climax is Mal 4:2, where the Messiah is named the Sun of righteousness arising with healing in his wings — the light that not only shines but heals what it shines on. Ecclesiastes uses the sun differently, as the boundary of the merely natural life: everything done under the sun, considered without reference to God, is vanity, and “there is no new thing under the sun” (Ecc 1:9). Finally, the sun is provisional. In the city of God there is no need of it, for the glory of God lightens it and the Lamb is the light thereof; the lamp is put out when the day it served has fully come.
webster_summary: The greater light, made on the fourth day to rule the day and to mark signs and seasons; a creature and never a deity, the emblem of God's constancy and common mercy, of Christ as the Sun of righteousness, and of the bounded natural life in Ecclesiastes.
webster_full: SUN, n. 1. The splendid orb or luminary which, being in or near the center of our system of worlds, gives light and heat to all the planets.
2. In Scripture, the sun is the greater light appointed to rule the day, and with the moon and stars to be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years. Genesis 1.
3. That which resembles the sun in brightness or in beneficence. The LORD God is a sun and shield. Psalm 84. The Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings. Malachi 4.
4. Under the sun; on the earth; in this present world, considered apart from what is above it. There is no new thing under the sun. Eccles. 1.

5. The worship of the sun was the most ancient and general of the idolatries, and is expressly forbidden in the law, which warns against lifting up the eyes unto the sun and being driven to worship them. Deut. 4.
scriptures: Psalm 84:11
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
Malachi 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Ecclesiastes 1:9
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
Matthew 5:45
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
corruption_summary: The oldest idolatry is sun worship, and its modern form is not a temple but a premise — that the sun and its system are self-explaining, so that the creature that Genesis refuses to name as a god is made the ultimate explanation instead.
corruption_paragraphs: The law names this corruption before it happened and forbids it by anticipation: Israel was warned lest they lift up their eyes unto heaven and, seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, be driven to worship and serve them. Ezekiel saw the abomination in the temple itself — five and twenty men with their backs toward the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east, worshipping the sun. Josiah's reformation had to take away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun. This is not a quaint ancient error; it is the permanent instinct of the fallen heart to worship what it can see, and it recurs wherever the visible order is treated as ultimate.

The current form of the error keeps the sun's brightness and drops the Maker. A naturalism that presents the solar system as its own sufficient explanation performs exactly the substitution Rom 1:25 describes — serving the creature more than the Creator — while claiming to have escaped religion altogether. Genesis had already answered it by refusing the sun a name and by making light on the first day, before the lamp existed to carry it. The Christian therefore is free to study the sun as thoroughly as he pleases, and free from any obligation to treat it as ultimate; it is a servant, and it is going out when its work is done.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemesh is the ordinary name of the luminary, pointedly avoided in the Genesis creation account. Greek hēlios supplies the New Testament term. A separate Hebrew word, chammâh, names the sun poetically as the hot one.
roots_lines: Hebrew shemesh (H8121) — sun; some 134 occurrences. Note its absence from Gen 1:16, where Moses says only “the greater light,” declining the name the nations had deified.
Hebrew chammâh (H2535) — the sun as the hot one, from chāmam, to be warm; the poetic term in Isa 30:26, where the light of the sun shall be sevenfold.
Hebrew 'ōr (H216) — light; made on the first day, before the sun on the fourth, so that light is shewn to be independent of its later vessel.
Greek hēlios (G2246) — sun; used of the sun darkened at the crucifixion (Luk 23:45) and of the face of the Son of man shining as the sun in his strength (Rev 1:16).
Greek anatolē (G395) — a rising, the east, the dayspring; the word of Luk 1:78, “the dayspring from on high hath visited us,” joining the sunrise figure to the incarnation.
usage: Of the creature ruling the day: the greater light (Gen 1:16); the sun shall not smite thee by day (Psa 121:6); he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mat 5:45).
Of God and of Christ figuratively: the LORD God is a sun and shield (Psa 84:11); the Sun of righteousness with healing in his wings (Mal 4:2); his countenance as the sun shineth (Rev 1:16).
Of the bounded natural life in Ecclesiastes: labour under the sun, no new thing under the sun, vanity under the sun — the phrase marking life reckoned without reference to what is above it.

etymology: From Old English mōna, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root meaning to measure — the same root that gives month, measure, and Latin mēnsis. The moon is named for its office: it is the great measurer, the clock hung in the sky. Hebrew has two words, yārēach (the ordinary name, tied to yerach, a month) and the poetic lebānâh, the white one. As with the sun, Genesis withholds the name on the fourth day and says only “the lesser light to rule the night” — a deliberate refusal to use the word the nations had made into a god.
biblical_def: The moon is the lesser light, made on the fourth day to rule the night and to serve, with the sun and stars, for signs and for seasons. Its borrowed brightness makes it the fitting emblem of derived and dependent glory: it rules, but it rules by reflection, having no light in itself. Israel's calendar hung on it, since the month began with the new moon and the feasts were reckoned from the months, so that the moon governed when the nation would assemble and worship. David makes it an argument for humility — “When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; what is man, that thou art mindful of him?” (Psa 8:3-4) — where the vastness of the ordained lights magnifies the condescension of God toward a creature so small. The same ordained regularity becomes the ground of covenant assurance: the LORD gives the moon and stars for a light by night, and only if those ordinances depart shall the seed of Israel cease from being a nation. In the prophets the moon turned to blood is a sign of the great and terrible day of the LORD (Joe 2:31), quoted by Peter at Pentecost. Paul draws the last lesson: the glory of the moon differs from the glory of the sun and from the glory of the stars, and so it shall be in the resurrection (1Co 15:41) — glory is real, ordered, and unequal, and none of it is self-generated.
webster_summary: The lesser light, made to rule the night and to measure the months; a creature shining by borrowed light, governing Israel's calendar of feasts, a witness to God's ordained constancy, and a sign in the prophets of the day of the LORD.
webster_full: MOON, n. 1. The heavenly orb which revolves round the earth; a satellite of the earth. She rules the night by reflecting the light of the sun.
2. In Scripture, the lesser light appointed to rule the night, and with the sun and the stars to be for signs and for seasons. Genesis 1.
3. A month; the period of the moon's revolution. The word month is from moon, and in the Hebrew likewise, yerach a month from yareach the moon.
4. New moon; the beginning of the month, announced in Israel by the sound of trumpets and marked by appointed offerings. Numbers 10; Psalm 81.
5. The worship of the moon, as of the queen of heaven, was among the idolatries into which Israel fell, and was expressly rebuked by the prophet Jeremiah. Jer. 44.
scriptures: Psalm 8:3
When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained;
Psalm 121:6
The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night.
Joel 2:31
The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come.
1 Corinthians 15:41
There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory.
corruption_summary: The moon was worshipped in the ancient world as the queen of heaven and is consulted in ours as a source of guidance and mood; both are the same refusal to let the lesser light be lesser.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah records the plainest instance of the ancient error. The women of Judah in Egypt told the prophet outright that they would burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as their fathers had done, and that they had been better off when they did. Moon worship was not a fringe superstition but a household religion with a domestic economy attached, and God judged it. The law had already forbidden it by name, and Job disclaims it as a heart sin — if I beheld the moon walking in brightness, and my heart hath been secretly enticed, this were an iniquity to be punished by the judge.

The modern residue is astrology, in which the phases of the moon are read for temperament, fortune, and timing. It is worth naming plainly rather than smiling at, because Scripture treats it as a rival source of guidance, and Isaiah's mockery of the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, is aimed exactly here. The Christian answer is not that the moon has no influence on tides and seasons, which it plainly has, but that it has no word. Guidance comes by Scripture and providence, from a God who speaks; the lights were given for signs and seasons, not for oracles.
roots_summary: Hebrew yārēach is the ordinary name and is tied directly to yerach, a month; lebānâh is the poetic white one. Greek selēnē supplies the New Testament term, and the related verb gives the Gospels' word for those afflicted at the moon's changes.
roots_lines: Hebrew yārēach (H3394) — moon; some 27 occurrences, absent from Gen 1:16 where Moses says only “the lesser light.”
Hebrew lebānâh (H3842) — the moon as the white one, from lāban, to be white; the poetic term of Son 6:10 and Isa 24:23.
Hebrew chōdesh (H2320) — new moon, and thence the month; the day of the moon's renewal, kept with trumpets and offerings.
Greek selēnē (G4582) — moon; used in Act 2:20 of the moon turned into blood and in Rev 12:1 of the woman with the moon under her feet.

Greek selēniazomai (G4583) — to be moonstruck, rendered lunatick in Mat 4:24 and 17:15; the Authorized Version preserves the ancient association of the moon with these afflictions without endorsing it as their cause.
usage: Of the creature ruling the night: the lesser light (Gen 1:16); nor the moon by night (Psa 121:6); the moon and the stars which thou hast ordained (Psa 8:3).
Of the calendar of worship: the new moon and the sabbath (Isa 66:23; Col 2:16); blowing the trumpet in the new moon (Psa 81:3).
Of prophetic sign: the moon turned into blood (Joe 2:31; Act 2:20); the moon shall not give her light (Mat 24:29); the moon confounded when the LORD reigns in Zion (Isa 24:23).

etymology: From Old English steorra, common Germanic, cognate with Latin stella and Greek astēr. Genesis dispatches the entire host of them in four words — “he made the stars also” — an almost dismissive clause appended to the fourth day, and again the polemic is deliberate: the bodies that ruled the destinies of men in Babylonian religion are an afterthought in Moses' account, made by the same hand that made the lamps and hung in the same firmament.
biblical_def: The stars are creatures of the fourth day, innumerable to men and individually known to God: “He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psa 147:4). That verse is the whole doctrine in miniature — what is beyond counting to us is a named roll to Him, and the psalm sets it immediately beside His healing of the broken in heart, so that the God of the galaxies and the God of the wounded are shewn to be one God with one attention. To Abraham the stars became the sign of the promise, when God brought him forth and bade him tell them if he were able, and said, So shall thy seed be — a promise counted to him for righteousness. The star is also messianic: Balaam prophesied a Star out of Jacob, and the wise men said, “we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him” (Mat 2:2), coming to the child rather than to the sky. The Lord Jesus takes the title to Himself at the close of the canon: “I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star” (Rev 22:16). Finally the stars are the figure of the saints' glory. They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever (Dan 12:3); and since one star differeth from another star in glory, the resurrection glory of the saints is real, ordered, and not uniform.
webster_summary: The innumerable lights of the fourth day, each named and numbered by God; the sign of the promise to Abraham, the emblem of Christ as the bright and morning star, and the figure of the saints shining in resurrection glory.
webster_full: STAR, n. 1. Any of the luminous bodies which appear in the heavens, and are supposed to be suns, each with its own system. He made the stars also. Genesis 1.
2. In Scripture, the stars are used as the emblem of a multitude beyond numbering. Tell the stars, if thou be able to number them; so shall thy seed be. Genesis 15.
3. A figure of Christ. There shall come a Star out of Jacob. Numbers 24. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star. Rev. 22.
4. A figure of ministers and of the saints. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches. Rev. 1. They that turn many to righteousness shall shine as the stars for ever and ever. Dan. 12.
5. The reading of the stars for the foretelling of events, called astrology, is the vain art of the Chaldeans, which the prophet derides and the law forbids. Isa. 47; Deut. 18.
scriptures: Psalm 147:4
He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.
Matthew 2:2
Saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him.
Daniel 12:3
And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.
Revelation 22:16
I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.
corruption_summary: Astrology — the reading of the stars for guidance and destiny — is the corruption Scripture names most often and mocks most sharply, and it survives undiminished as entertainment that is still consulted in earnest.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah's taunt against Babylon is the sharpest thing in Scripture on the subject: let now the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, stand up and save thee from these things that shall come upon thee; behold, they shall be as stubble, the fire shall burn them. The mockery is aimed at a professional class that governed an empire's decisions. Daniel's narrative makes the same point by demonstration — the Chaldean astrologers could not tell the king his dream, and God's servant could, because there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets. The law forbids the practice with the other divinations of the nations, and Deu 4:19 explains the reason: the host of heaven was divided unto all nations as a gift, not appointed as an oracle.

It is objected that nobody takes horoscopes seriously now, and the objection understates how far the practice has revived. The claim being made is a real one — that character and future are written in the stars at birth — and it is a rival doctrine of providence, assigning to creatures the government that belongs to the Creator, and to fate the place that belongs to a Father. The star of Bethlehem is the exact counter-example that is usually cited in defence of the art: it did not disclose the future to the wise men, and it was not read by their skill; God moved a light to bring worshippers to His Son. The sign served the Word and led men to Christ, which is the opposite of what astrology does.
roots_summary: Hebrew kōkhāb covers every star and constellation, and is the word of Abraham's promise and Balaam's prophecy. Greek distinguishes astēr, the single star, from astron, the constellation or star-group.
roots_lines: Hebrew kōkhāb (H3556) — star; some 37 occurrences, including the Star out of Jacob (Num 24:17) and the morning stars singing together (Job 38:7).
Hebrew tsābā' (H6635) — host; in the phrase the host of heaven, the stars considered as an ordered army, whence the divine title LORD of hosts.
Hebrew mazzālōth (H4208) — the twelve signs, the constellations of the zodiac; named in 2Ki 23:5 among the idolatries Josiah put down.
Greek astēr (G792) — a star; the word of the star in the east (Mat 2:2) and of the seven stars in the Lord's right hand (Rev 1:16).
Greek phōsphōros (G5459) — the light-bringer, the day star; used in 2Pe 1:19 of the day star arising in the heart, joined to the more sure word of prophecy.
usage: Of the created host: he made the stars also (Gen 1:16); he telleth the number of the stars (Psa 147:4); the host of heaven cannot be numbered (Jer 33:22).
Of the promise and the Messiah: so shall thy seed be (Gen 15:5); a Star out of Jacob (Num 24:17); we have seen his star in the east (Mat 2:2).
Of ministers and saints: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches (Rev 1:20); shining as the stars for ever and ever (Dan 12:3); one star differeth from another star in glory (1Co 15:41).

etymology: From Old English clūd, which meant a mass of rock or a hill — the sense transferred to the piled mass of vapour by likeness of shape, so that the word for a crag became the word for a thunderhead. The Hebrew 'ānān is the covering cloud, and it is the word used of the pillar and of the glory; 'āb is the thick dark cloud of storm. Scripture's clouds are rarely weather and almost always presence.
biblical_def: In Scripture the cloud is chiefly the veil of the divine presence — the means by which a holy God comes near to a people who could not survive seeing Him plainly. The LORD went before Israel “in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way” (Exo 13:21), the same pillar that stood between the camp and the Egyptians, darkness to one and light to the other. When the tabernacle was finished the cloud covered the tent and the glory filled it, so that Moses was not able to enter; the cloud is thus both revelation and mercy, shewing that God is there and shielding the creature from what he cannot bear. The same cloud filled Solomon's temple, overshadowed the mount of transfiguration with the Father's voice out of it, and received the Lord out of the disciples' sight at the ascension (Act 1:9). And the promise of His return is in the same terms: this same Jesus shall so come in like manner, and every eye shall see him coming in the clouds of heaven. The cloud is also the emblem of the small beginning of great mercy — Elijah's servant saw only “a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand” (1Ki 18:44), and that hand-sized cloud broke a three-year drought. Hebrews turns the figure to the saints: we are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1), a company so numerous that it is described as weather.
webster_summary: The visible veil of the divine presence — the pillar that led Israel, the glory that filled tabernacle and temple, the overshadowing at the transfiguration, the chariot of the ascension and of the second coming — and the figure both of a small beginning of mercy and of the encompassing company of the saints.
webster_full: CLOUD, n. 1. A collection of visible vapor, or watery particles, suspended in the atmosphere at some altitude.
2. In Scripture, the symbol and covering of the divine presence. The LORD went before them in a pillar of a cloud. Exodus 13. A cloud filled the house of the LORD. 1 Kings 8.
3. A great multitude; a collection so numerous as to resemble a cloud. So great a cloud of witnesses. Heb. 12.
4. That which obscures, darkens, or threatens; whence a cloud upon the countenance, and the day of clouds and thick darkness in the prophets. Joel 2.
5. To come in the clouds; the manner of our Lord's ascension and of his promised return. Behold, he cometh with clouds, and every eye shall see him. Rev. 1.
scriptures: Exodus 13:21
And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to go by day and night:
1 Kings 18:44

And it came to pass at the seventh time, that he said, Behold, there ariseth a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand. And he said, Go up, say unto Ahab, Prepare thy chariot, and get thee down, that the rain stop thee not.
Acts 1:9
And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.
Hebrews 12:1

corruption_summary: The cloud of glory is commonly reduced to a piece of ancient stage-scenery or a natural phenomenon dressed up by later writers, which empties the exodus, the temple, the transfiguration, and the ascension of the one thing they are all reporting.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern treatment explains the pillar of cloud as a volcanic plume, a caravan brazier, or a literary device added long after the events to lend authority to the sanctuary. Each of these begins from the assumption that God does not come near His people visibly, and then reconstructs the text to fit. Scripture presents the cloud as an event with witnesses, consequences, and a schedule — it moved and the camp moved, it settled and the camp stayed, it filled the house so that the priests could not stand to minister. The narrative is not decorated with the cloud; the narrative depends on it. Once the cloud is explained away, the exodus becomes a migration, the tabernacle becomes architecture, and the ascension becomes a way of saying the disciples felt encouraged.

There is a second and gentler misuse inside the church: treating the cloud as a mood. Where the glory-cloud is invoked to describe an atmosphere in a meeting, or a sense of presence produced by music and expectation, the biblical thing is exchanged for a feeling that can be manufactured. The Scriptural cloud does not respond to technique; it comes and goes at God's appointment, it silences rather than excites, and it is consistently associated with the fear of the LORD. The Christian's access now is better than a cloud and not less — through the veil, that is to say, Christ's flesh — and the writer to the Hebrews sets the two side by side deliberately: not the mount that burned with fire and blackness and darkness and tempest, but mount Sion, and the city of the living God.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ānān is the covering cloud of the pillar and the glory; 'āb is the thick storm cloud; 'arāphel is the thick darkness in which God is said to dwell. Greek nephelē is the single cloud, nephos the mass, used of the cloud of witnesses.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ānān (H6051) — cloud; the word of the pillar (Exo 13:21), of the cloud on the mercy seat (Lev 16:2), and of the glory filling the house.
Hebrew 'āb (H5645) — a thick dark cloud, the storm mass; the little cloud of 1Ki 18:44 and the clouds that are the dust of His feet (Nah 1:3).
Hebrew 'arāphel (H6205) — gross darkness, thick cloud; “the LORD said that he would dwell in the thick darkness” (1Ki 8:12).
Greek nephelē (G3507) — a cloud, a single defined cloud; the overshadowing cloud of the transfiguration and the cloud that received Him at the ascension.
Greek nephos (G3509) — a cloud mass; used once only, of the great cloud of witnesses in Heb 12:1, where the plural company is pictured as a single encompassing bank.
usage: Of the guiding and covering presence: the pillar of a cloud (Exo 13:21); the cloud covering the tent of the congregation (Exo 40:34); the cloud filling the house of the LORD (1Ki 8:10).
Of the coming and going of the Son: a bright cloud overshadowed them (Mat 17:5); a cloud received him out of their sight (Act 1:9); behold, he cometh with clouds (Rev 1:7).
Figuratively of multitude and of transience: so great a cloud of witnesses (Heb 12:1); your goodness is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away (Hos 6:4).
